title: The Surprising Effectivenessof Shared Memory in Looped Transformers

paper.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Shared Memory in Looped Transformers
paper.abstract: Abstract Looped Transformers apply the same layers several times per token, adding compute to improve quality without more parameters. Each recursion, however, writes its own key-value cache, so memory still grows with compute. Inference-time techniques can shrink this cache at a cost in quality. We pretrain looped language models to share memory: only the first recursion writes a cache, and later recursions read it while keeping a short window of their own. Surprisingly, we find that sharing memory does not cost quality and instead improves it. At 150M–1B parameters, our Looped Prediction Transformer ( lpt ) and its hybrid variant set a new quality–memory frontier for looped models: with five recursions, the hybrid lowers validation perplexity on FineWeb-Edu by 1.12 1.12 – 1.82 1.82 relative to a same-size standard Transformer while using 76 76 – 79 % 79\% less context memory. Through an extensive analysis, we investigate why memory sharing helps. Shared and local memory develop different representations, and later recursions attend mostly to the shared memory, which also acts as a gradient highway to the first recursion.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Looped Transformers ( lt ) repeatedly apply the same layers several times before predicting the next token, adding computation without adding parameters ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . In principle, they trade time for memory, matching the compute of a larger model with far fewer parameters. In standard formulations, however, context memory still grows with recursion depth, as each iteration keeps a separate key-value (KV) cache ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . At long contexts, this context memory can grow larger than the weights memory itself, undoing the very reason to use a looped model. Sharing caches across recursions during decoding can save substantial memory with little quality loss ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . So far, this reuse has been studied mainly as a way to save memory. Yet it also shows that memory written by one recursion can serve the others, even in models never trained to share it. This raises a question: if sharing can work untrained, what can it do when models are trained for it? To answer it, we train looped models with memory sharing from the start, investigating it as an architectural inductive bias. We study a simple recipe for Memory Sharing in looped Transformers ( Figure 1 , left). At each full-attention layer, later recursions attend to both their own KV entries and the cache written by that layer in the first recursion, within the same attention operation. To further save memory, we truncate the cache of every recursion after the first to a short sliding window. The resulting Looped Prediction Transformer ( lpt ) keeps lt ’s sequential recurrence and uses context memory close to a standard (non-looped) Transformer’s. Applied to the full-attention layers of a hybrid looped Transformer ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , the same rule yields the Hybrid Looped Prediction Transformer ( h-lpt ). We pretrain all models from scratch at 150 150 M to 1 1 B parameters. Because later recursions give up most of their own memory, one would expect Memory Sharing to cost some quality, as untrained sharing does. Surprisingly, Memory Sharing improves quality over full-cache lt even when each later recursion’s own cache covers less than 2 % 2\% of the context. Its advantage grows with depth: lt stops improving in perplexity after three recursions, while lpt improves through five. Across sizes, lpt lowers validation perplexity by up to 1.09 1.09 nats and raises downstream accuracy by up to 4.8 4.8 percentage points over a matched-depth lt , with up to 4.7 × 4.7\times less context memory and nearly the same inference FLOPs. Sharing also improves the hybrid baseline: at five recursions, h-lpt outperforms a same-size standard Transformer in both language modeling and downstream accuracy while using 76 76 – 79 % 79\% less context memory, moving the quality–memory frontier for looped models ( Figure 2 ). These results raise a further question: why does memory sharing improve quality? We find that later recursions rely heavily on the shared memory. lpt outperforms lt at every window size, even when later recursions keep no cache of their own, and later recursions attend mostly to shared memory even when their own cache covers the full context. Shared and local memory also develop distinct key representations, suggesting that they serve different purposes. Reading shared memory sends gradients directly to the first recursion, helping it learn what to store. This gradient highway bypasses the intermediate recursions: in lt , the magnitude of the gradient reaching the first recursion falls sharply with depth, while lpt recovers much of it through the shared memory. When we block this path, the model still reads shared memory but no longer matches lpt ’s quality and stability.

sections.heading: 3 Looping with Shared Memory
sections.text: We study Memory Sharing , in which later recursions read the memory written by the first recursion, as an inductive bias for looped models. The first recursion runs as in lt and writes a full-context cache 𝒞 ( 1 ) \mathcal{C}^{(1)} at each layer, and every later recursion attends to this cache together with its own KV entries, using a single softmax. To also keep looping memory-efficient, we restrict each later recursion’s own cache to a short window. The first recursion therefore acts as a memory phase that builds the model’s only full-context memory, while later recursions use it to refine the prediction. We refer to the first recursion as the state recursion and to the later ones as prediction recursions , and call the resulting model the Looped Prediction Transformer ( lpt ; Figure 1 ). Like lt , lpt applies the same L L -layer stack R R times and passes the final output to the language-modeling head ( Equation 1 ). Let ω \omega be the number of preceding positions kept in each prediction recursion’s window, and write 𝒞 [ i − ω , i ] ( t ) \mathcal{C}_{[i-\omega,i]}^{(t)} for the entries from positions i − ω i-\omega through i i , including the current entry. The state recursion reads its own cache, as in lt ( Equation 2 ). A prediction recursion reads the shared memory together with its own window. The entries read by a query at position i i in recursion t t are 𝒜 lpt ( t ) ​ ( i ) = { 𝒞 ≤ i ( 1 ) , t = 1 , 𝒞 ≤ i ( 1 ) ∪ 𝒞 [ i − ω , i ] ( t ) , t = 2 , … , R . \mathcal{A}_{\text{{lpt}}}^{(t)}(i)=\begin{cases}\mathcal{C}_{\leq i}^{(1)},&t=1,\\ \mathcal{C}_{\leq i}^{(1)}\cup\mathcal{C}_{[i-\omega,i]}^{(t)},&t=2,\ldots,R.\end{cases} (3) In prediction recursions, the two sets are attended to using a single softmax. Setting ω = T \omega=T gives every prediction recursion a full-context cache of its own, as in lt , and leaves access to shared memory as the only difference between the two models; we use this setting in Section 6 to separate the effect of sharing from that of the short window. Memory Sharing also applies to looped hybrid Transformers, which interleave linear-attention and full-attention layers ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . The first recursion runs the hybrid as usual. In later recursions, each linear-attention layer keeps its own recurrent state, which is small and fixed in size, while each full-attention layer applies Equation 3 , as in lpt . Applied to lt2 ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , this gives h-lpt .

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: To study memory sharing, we compare lpt with lt and h-lpt with lt2 . We also compare with the Parallel Loop Transformer ( plt ) ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , which parallelizes recursions and uses gated dual attention over the first recursion’s shared cache and each later recursion’s local cache. Other baselines are a standard Transformer ( std ), loopie , which repeats each layer before advancing to the next ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and deepstd , a deeper, narrower Transformer without weight sharing that matches the looped models in effective depth and approximately in parameters.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text: All models use a decoder-only Transformer backbone with RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary positional embeddings, and tied input and output embeddings. We train S, M, and L models with approximately 150 150 M, 450 450 M, and 1 1 B parameters; the main comparisons cover all three sizes, and most ablations and analyses use S and M. The context length is 4,096 4{,}096 . Unless otherwise specified, lpt and h-lpt use a prediction window of ω = 64 \omega=64 . We study two, three, and five recursions. This range includes the two loop steps of loopie ( Gao et al., 2026 ) and surrounds the four recursions of Ouro and lt2 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . 1 1 1 Nine recursions bring instability in several model families and limited accuracy gains, consistent with the loss spikes Ouro reports at eight ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . We report these experiments in Appendix E . All models use nanoGPT’s default optimizer settings ( Karpathy, 2022 ) . Model dimensions, normalization, and training details are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Data and Training
sections.text: We pretrain on FineWeb-Edu ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) using 20 20 B tokens for S and M, and 50 50 B for L, roughly 2 2 – 7 × 7\times the Chinchilla compute-optimal token budgets ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . The main tables report one run per configuration, with the same initialization seed and data order across models. At S, we also train three more seeds per model and confirm that seed variation is far below the gaps we report ( Appendix B ). We study two training objectives. Final loss computes the next-token NLL at the final recursion only. Adaptive loss follows Ouro ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , weighting per-recursion NLLs with a learned per-token halting distribution and adding KL regularization. Unless otherwise specified, lt uses adaptive loss and all other models use final loss.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: We report perplexity on 10 10 M held-out FineWeb-Edu tokens and mean zero-shot accuracy on ARC-Easy ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) , SciQ ( Welbl et al., 2017 ) , and LAMBADA ( Paperno et al., 2016 ) , using the LM Evaluation Harness ( Gao et al., 2023 ) . We compute context memory and decoding FLOPs per generated token analytically at a 4,096 4{,}096 -token context, relative to the same size std . Context memory includes the KV cache and GDN’s recurrent state. Figure 2: lpt and h-lpt reach higher accuracy with much smaller caches than the looped baselines. sections.heading: Memory Sharing Improves Quality
sections.text: Restricting the memory written by later recursions could hurt prediction. Surprisingly, our Memory Sharing approach improves quality. At matched size and recursion count, lpt lowers validation perplexity by 0.38 0.38 – 1.09 1.09 and raises accuracy by 0.4 0.4 – 4.8 4.8 percentage points over lt , with 2.0 2.0 – 4.7 × 4.7\times less KV memory and under 1 % 1\% more FLOPs ( Table 1 ). Measured on an H100, the memory savings are the same, so lpt fits 2.0 2.0 – 4.8 × 4.8\times as many sequences in a batch as lt ( Appendix F ). The perplexity gain grows with recursion count ( Table 1 ): lt stops improving beyond three recursions at every size, while lpt continues to improve through five. At comparable cache sizes, lpt also reaches lower perplexity than plt ’s parallel formulation. When it comes to hybrid variants, h-lpt keeps this memory at 0.18 0.18 – 0.24 × 0.24\times std ’s across recursion counts, while lt2 ’s remaining full-attention caches still grow with depth, approaching std ’s context memory at five recursions. Despite these 2 2 – 4 × 4\times memory gains, h-lpt matches or outperforms lt2 in terms of quality at every recursion count. At five recursions, it lowers perplexity by 0.09 0.09 – 0.15 0.15 and raises accuracy by 0.8 0.8 – 1.2 1.2 points over lt2 , with 4.1 4.1 – 4.2 × 4.2\times less context memory and about 0.1 % 0.1\% more inference FLOPs. Incidentally, we note that for low recursion counts, the hybrid lt2 improves on lt while using less memory and compute. A factor that could explain this gap – and the instability of lt – is Ouro’s normalization, which we use for both lt and lpt . In Appendix C , we explore other normalizations that make lt more robust, but none of these variants matches lpt .

sections.heading: More Quality from the Same Parameters
sections.text: Both memory-sharing models improve on std with little additional memory, or much less for h-lpt ( Figure 2 ). At five recursions, lpt lowers perplexity by 1.03 1.03 – 1.92 1.92 and raises accuracy by 3.4 3.4 – 5.7 5.7 points with 6.25 % 6.25\% more context memory. h-lpt lowers perplexity by 1.12 1.12 – 1.82 1.82 and raises accuracy by 3.1 3.1 – 5.6 5.6 points with 76 76 – 79 % 79\% less memory. This smaller cache lets h-lpt fit 3.6 3.6 – 5.0 × 5.0\times as many sequences as std on one GPU. With three to five recursions, h-lpt lowers perplexity by 0.94 0.94 – 1.82 1.82 while beating or staying close to std ’s throughput ( 1.4 1.4 – 1.5 × 1.5\times at three, 81 81 – 88 % 88\% at five, Appendix F ). Both models’ accuracy gains grow from two to five recursions at every size. lpt also outperforms loopie and deepstd , neither of which improves consistently with depth. Takeaway 1. Through Memory Sharing, lpt and especially h-lpt improves the quality–memory frontier for looped models ( Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: 6 Why Memory Sharing Helps
sections.text: We use S- and M-size models with two, three, and five recursions to study why this inductive bias improves quality ( Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Memory Sharing Stabilizes Deep Recursion
sections.text: We compare final and adaptive loss in lt and lpt ( Figure 4 ). Without intermediate supervision, adding recursions consistently worsens lt ’s perplexity, and the model collapses to unigram-level loss at five recursions. lpt stays stable, and final loss lowers its perplexity by 0.16 0.16 – 0.50 0.50 compared with adaptive loss. Its intermediate recursions can refine the hidden state without having to predict early. Takeaway 2. lpt stays stable and trains best with final loss. sections.heading: Prediction Recursion Needs Local Memory
sections.text: We train lpt with prediction windows ranging from ω = 0 \omega=0 to the full context of 4,096 4{,}096 tokens ( Figure 4 ). lpt outperforms lt at every window size, across both sizes and all tested depths. This includes ω = 0 \omega=0 , where prediction recursions keep no local history and read shared memory alongside only their current KV entry. At the other extreme, ω = 4,096 \omega=4{,}096 , lt and lpt differ only in access to shared memory. lpt still lowers perplexity by 0.24 0.24 – 1.15 1.15 relative to lt with the better of its two training objectives at each depth, close to the 0.32 0.32 – 1.09 1.09 gain at ω = 64 \omega=64 . Overall, window size has a modest effect on quality, and what really matters is the access to the shared memory. To balance quality and efficiency, we adopt ω = 64 \omega=64 as the default for our memory sharing models. Takeaway 3. Shared memory improves quality across prediction-window sizes, even when later recursions keep no local history.

sections.heading: Later Recursions Attend More to Shared Memory
sections.text: We next measure how much attention is assigned to the shared memory in later recursions. We evaluate each model on the same 4,096 4{,}096 -token validation sequence and average the attention assigned to shared keys over queries and heads ( Figure 6 and Appendix D ). Shared memory receives most attention at every prediction recursion in both sizes. Its share is 57 57 – 71 % 71\% in earlier prediction recursions and rises to 73 73 – 80 % 80\% in the final recursion. 2 2 2 Additional comparisons in the appendix show that shared memory still receives most attention with full prediction caches, while adaptive loss makes its use more uniform across recursions ( Figure 11 ). Takeaway 4. Later recursions attend more to shared memory than to their own caches, with a stronger preference when getting closer to the prediction. sections.heading: Shared and Local Memory Develop Different Representations
sections.text: Shared keys serve every later recursion, whereas local keys serve only the recursion that writes them. To see whether these roles are reflected in their representations, we compare S-size lt and lpt with three recursions, both trained with final loss, the only tested setting with at least three recursions where lt trains with final loss without a substantial drop in quality ( Figure 4 ). We evaluate both models on the same 4,096 4{,}096 -token validation sequence and extract queries and keys before rotary encoding. We concatenate the attention heads and fit principal component analysis (PCA) jointly to queries and keys across tokens and recursions per model and layer ( Appendix D ). Shared and local keys consistently form distinct clusters in lpt , whereas keys from different recursions overlap more in lt ( Figure 6 ). In Appendix D , we show similar separation in lpt across S and M at three and five recursions ( Figure 10 ). We also show that with full prediction caches, the clusters overlap more but still remain distinguishable, even though shared and local keys cover the same positions ( Figure 9 ). Prior work attributes the small cost of cache reuse to the similarity of keys and values across recursions ( Bae et al., 2025 ) , as we see in lt . With Memory Sharing, shared and local keys are instead clearly different. This shows that representation similarity across layers is not a necessary condition for effective memory sharing. This also fits the freedom that final loss gives: recursions need not all produce prediction-ready states, so the first can specialize in building memory and the later ones in using it. This specialization may help explain the quality gains, similar to how Monea et al. (2026) show that Transformers benefit from assigning memory construction and next-token prediction to separate residual streams. Takeaway 5. Shared and local memory diverge in their local representations, so sharing is not reliant on recursions writing similar memories.

sections.heading: Shared Memory Is a Gradient Highway
sections.text: Reading shared memory gives the final loss a direct gradient path to the first recursion, bypassing the intermediate recursions. We evaluate the std , lt , and lpt models of Table 1 on the same 32 32 validation sequences of 4,096 4{,}096 tokens and backpropagate the final loss from 32 32 fixed positions in each. We measure each recursion’s contribution to the gradient on the Transformer block weights, and split the first recursion’s contribution into its hidden-state and shared-KV paths by repeating the backward pass with shared KV detached ( Appendix D ). In lt , the first-recursion gradient norm falls sharply with depth. lpt recovers much of the signal magnitude relative to the single-pass std reference, with a much smaller decline as depth increases ( Figure 8 ). At five recursions, most of this gradient comes through the shared KV cache. The same holds for lpt with adaptive loss or full prediction caches ( Figure 12 ). sections.heading: Separating Memory from Prediction
sections.text: In a standard Transformer, each hidden state does two jobs. It predicts the next token, and it writes the keys and values that later positions read. Several architectures separate these jobs across token streams, as in the two-stream attention of XLNet ( Yang et al., 2019 ) . The State-Prediction Separation Transformer ( Monea et al., 2026 ) gives memory construction and next-token prediction separate residual streams and improves language modeling, and Langford et al. (2026) study a variant of this split. A second family separates them across layers. The first layers write one cache once, and the remaining layers only read it ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; Capps, 2026 ) . Instead, lpt decouples memory from prediction across the recursions of a looped Transformer: the first recursion writes the model’s only full-context memory, and every later recursion reads it while it predicts, keeping just a short window of its own. Looped models thus offer a third place for the split, with no extra stream or layer, and our analysis finds evidence that the recursions learn these roles ( Section 6 ).

sections.heading: Looped Transformers and Memory Sharing
sections.text: Looped Transformers apply the same layers several times ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and recent work differs in which layers repeat and how recursions connect ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Mozer et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . In standard formulations, each recursion writes its own KV cache, so context memory grows with depth ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Sharing a cache across recursions, like sharing it across layers ( Brandon et al., 2024 ) , has been studied as a way to save memory. Without retraining, Huginn ( Geiping et al., 2025 ) reuses caches cyclically with little quality loss, and Ouro ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) can keep only the final or an averaged cache. Keeping only the first recursion’s cache sharply reduces Ouro’s quality, which suggests that shared memory has to be trained. Trained variants reuse the first recursion’s keys and values at a slight cost in quality ( Bae et al., 2025 ) , compute them once in a separate prelude ( Capps, 2026 ) , or learn gated or compressed caches ( Vendrell et al., 2026 ; O’Neill and Reid, 2026 ) . plt ( Wu et al., 2025 ) has the closest design to ours, although it focuses on parallelizing recursions. It shares the first recursion’s cache with gated local caches and runs recursions in parallel, while lpt keeps them sequential and reads both caches in one softmax. We find that lpt performs better. All of these treat sharing as a cost to contain. We instead treat it as an inductive bias that separates memory from prediction and show that it improves quality ( Section 5 and Section 6 ).

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: We investigate memory sharing as an architectural inductive bias for looped models, and find that it not only cuts context memory but also improves quality in both full attention and hybrid models. Our Memory Sharing lpt models achieve consistently better perplexity and downstream accuracy than their usual looped counterparts, while matching the KV cache memory of a standard non-looped model. Our analyses suggest that sharing helps recursions learn different roles. The first recursion builds memory that later recursions use to refine the prediction. Those reads also give the final loss a direct gradient path to the first recursion. The different representations of shared and local memory support this division of roles, and cutting this gradient path hurts learning. Shared memory changes how later recursions read information and how the first recursion learns to write it. Overall, our findings suggest that shared memory is a useful inductive bias for looped models, helping them make better use of computation within a limited memory budget.

sections.heading: Limitations & Future work
sections.text: Like other looped Transformers, lpt is not compute-optimal: it trades time for quality, but unlike lt , its memory barely grows with depth. At five recursions it costs 4.3 4.3 – 4.8 × 4.8\times the decoding FLOPs of std , about the same as lt , and it spends the same number of recursions on every token. Choosing that number per token is future work. All our comparisons are parameter-matched, including deepstd , and we do not train a standard Transformer matched in decoding FLOPs instead, which at five recursions would have several times the parameters. We train up to 1 1 B parameters on one corpus with 4,096 4{,}096 -token contexts and do not test long-context tasks or, given our limited pretraining, very advanced tasks. Our analyses use S and M models, since not every configuration they need was trained at L, and only the detach ablation looks at training dynamics. Both the stability and memory improvements of lpt are promising for effectively scaling looped models to higher recursion counts. More sophisticated Memory Sharing approaches could also be explored in future work, such as increasing the number of state recursions or alternating state recursions and prediction recursions.

sections.heading: Attention Implementation
sections.text: During training, each prediction recursion concatenates its keys and values with the shared keys and values along the sequence dimension, separately at each full-attention layer. A block mask implements Equation 3 , allowing full causal attention over shared entries and causal sliding-window attention over local entries. FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) skips fully masked blocks.

sections.heading: Data Processing
sections.text: We tokenize with the GPT-2 tokenizer ( Radford et al., 2019 ) and pack documents into 4,096 4{,}096 -token sequences, inserting an end-of-sequence token between documents. Attention is masked across document boundaries, and boundary tokens are excluded from the language-modeling loss.

sections.heading: Optimization
sections.text: We use AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , and gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 . The global batch contains 96 96 sequences of 4,096 4{,}096 tokens, and training uses bfloat16 mixed precision. For L-size models, AdamW optimizer state is sharded across DDP ranks (ZeRO-1). The learning rate increases linearly to 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} over the first 50 50 M tokens, stays constant, then decreases linearly to 6 × 10 − 5 6\times 10^{-5} over the final 10 % 10\% of training. These are nanoGPT’s default optimizer settings, used unchanged for every model, size, and objective: we did not tune the learning rate or the warmup for any model, and we did not test whether a lower peak learning rate or a longer warmup changes how final-loss lt trains at depth ( Figure 4 ). For adaptive loss, we use Ouro’s adaptive-exit objective ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . A learned per-token halting distribution weights the losses across recursions, with a KL regularization weight of 0.1 0.1 . Final loss applies the language-modeling loss only at the last recursion.

sections.heading: Appendix F Decoding Speed and Memory on a GPU
sections.text: We test whether the analytic memory savings translate into larger batches and higher decoding throughput on a GPU. A smaller cache lets more sequences share a GPU, which can raise throughput ( Brandon et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) . As O’Neill and Reid (2026) do for a looped model, we measure the largest batch that fits at a fixed context and the throughput at that batch.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We decode on one NVIDIA H100 with 80 80 GB of memory, in bf16, at a 4,096 4{,}096 -token context: each step generates one token per sequence from a cache already filled to 4,068 4{,}068 tokens. All models share one decoding implementation in PyTorch: a preallocated cache per attention layer, FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) for attention, and CUDA graphs that replay a whole decoding step, all recursions and layers included. A later recursion of lpt or h-lpt attends to its shared and local caches in one softmax, which we compute by merging the two FlexAttention outputs by their log-sum-exp. Gated DeltaNet layers update their recurrent state one token at a time, with the kernels of flash-linear-attention ( Yang and Zhang, 2024 ) . std runs the same code with one recursion, and lt runs all its recursions, without early exit. Weights are random, since speed and memory do not depend on them. On the same GPU, decoding reproduces the full forward pass to bf16 precision. The maximum batch is the largest batch whose decoding steps run without running out of memory, and we measure throughput at this batch, or at 95 % 95\% of it when the CUDA graph does not fit. These measurements come from one research implementation, not an optimized serving engine, which would change the absolute speeds. Every model runs the same code, so the comparison holds within this implementation.

Each recursion, however, writes its own key-value cache, so memory still grows with compute. Inference-time techniques can shrink this cache at a cost in quality. We pretrain looped language models to share memory: only the first recursion writes a cache, and later recursions read it while keeping a short window of their own. Surprisingly, we find that sharing memory does not cost quality and instead improves it. At 150M–1B parameters, our Looped Prediction Transformer ( lpt ) and its hybrid variant set a new quality–memory frontier for looped models: with five recursions, the hybrid lowers validation perplexity on FineWeb-Edu by 1.12 1.12 – 1.82 1.82 relative to a same-size standard Transformer while using 76 76 – 79 % 79\% less context memory. Through an extensive analysis, we investigate why memory sharing helps. Shared and local memory develop different representations, and later recursions attend mostly to the shared memory, which also acts as a gradient highway to the first recursion. 1 1 footnotetext: Work done during an internship at IBM Research. Right: perplexity and context memory of 1 1 B-parameter models with two to five recursions, against a parameter-matched standard Transformer ( std ). Each of our models adds shared memory to the looped baseline above it: lpt to the looped Transformer lt , and h-lpt to the gated DeltaNet hybrid lt2 . 1 Introduction Looped Transformers ( lt ) repeatedly apply the same layers several times before predicting the next token, adding computation without adding parameters ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . In principle, they trade time for memory, matching the compute of a larger model with far fewer parameters. In standard formulations, however, context memory still grows with recursion depth, as each iteration keeps a separate key-value (KV) cache ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . At long contexts, this context memory can grow larger than the weights memory itself, undoing the very reason to use a looped model. Sharing caches across recursions during decoding can save substantial memory with little quality loss ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . So far, this reuse has been studied mainly as a way to save memory. Yet it also shows that memory written by one recursion can serve the others, even in models never trained to share it. This raises a question: if sharing can work untrained, what can it do when models are trained for it? To answer it, we train looped models with memory sharing from the start, investigating it as an architectural inductive bias. We study a simple recipe for Memory Sharing in looped Transformers ( Figure 1 , left). At each full-attention layer, later recursions attend to both their own KV entries and the cache written by that layer in the first recursion, within the same attention operation. To further save memory, we truncate the cache of every recursion after the first to a short sliding window. The resulting Looped Prediction Transformer ( lpt ) keeps lt ’s sequential recurrence and uses context memory close to a standard (non-looped) Transformer’s. Applied to the full-attention layers of a hybrid looped Transformer ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , the same rule yields the Hybrid Looped Prediction Transformer ( h-lpt ). We pretrain all models from scratch at 150 150 M to 1 1 B parameters. Because later recursions give up most of their own memory, one would expect Memory Sharing to cost some quality, as untrained sharing does. Surprisingly, Memory Sharing improves quality over full-cache lt even when each later recursion’s own cache covers less than 2 % 2\% of the context. Its advantage grows with depth: lt stops improving in perplexity after three recursions, while lpt improves through five. Across sizes, lpt lowers validation perplexity by up to 1.09 1.09 nats and raises downstream accuracy by up to 4.8 4.8 percentage points over a matched-depth lt , with up to 4.7 × 4.7\times less context memory and nearly the same inference FLOPs. Sharing also improves the hybrid baseline: at five recursions, h-lpt outperforms a same-size standard Transformer in both language modeling and downstream accuracy while using 76 76 – 79 % 79\% less context memory, moving the quality–memory frontier for looped models ( Figure 2 ). These results raise a further question: why does memory sharing improve quality? We find that later recursions rely heavily on the shared memory. lpt outperforms lt at every window size, even when later recursions keep no cache of their own, and later recursions attend mostly to shared memory even when their own cache covers the full context. Shared and local memory also develop distinct key representations, suggesting that they serve different purposes. Reading shared memory sends gradients directly to the first recursion, helping it learn what to store. This gradient highway bypasses the intermediate recursions: in lt , the magnitude of the gradient reaching the first recursion falls sharply with depth, while lpt recovers much of it through the shared memory. When we block this path, the model still reads shared memory but no longer matches lpt ’s quality and stability. 2 Looped Transformers A standard lt shares its weights across recursions, while each recursion computes its own hidden states and KV entries. We also compare with the Parallel Loop Transformer ( plt ) ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , which parallelizes recursions and uses gated dual attention over the first recursion’s shared cache and each later recursion’s local cache. Other baselines are a standard Transformer ( std ), loopie , which repeats each layer before advancing to the next ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and deepstd , a deeper, narrower Transformer without weight sharing that matches the looped models in effective depth and approximately in parameters. Architecture All models use a decoder-only Transformer backbone with RMSNorm, SwiGLU, rotary positional embeddings, and tied input and output embeddings. We train S, M, and L models with approximately 150 150 M, 450 450 M, and 1 1 B parameters; the main comparisons cover all three sizes, and most ablations and analyses use S and M. The context length is 4,096 4{,}096 . Unless otherwise specified, lpt and h-lpt use a prediction window of ω = 64 \omega=64 . We study two, three, and five recursions. This range includes the two loop steps of loopie ( Gao et al., 2026 ) and surrounds the four recursions of Ouro and lt2 ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . 1 1 1 Nine recursions bring instability in several model families and limited accuracy gains, consistent with the loss spikes Ouro reports at eight ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Surprisingly, our Memory Sharing approach improves quality. At matched size and recursion count, lpt lowers validation perplexity by 0.38 0.38 – 1.09 1.09 and raises accuracy by 0.4 0.4 – 4.8 4.8 percentage points over lt , with 2.0 2.0 – 4.7 × 4.7\times less KV memory and under 1 % 1\% more FLOPs ( Table 1 ). The perplexity gain grows with recursion count ( Table 1 ): lt stops improving beyond three recursions at every size, while lpt continues to improve through five. At comparable cache sizes, lpt also reaches lower perplexity than plt ’s parallel formulation. Shared and Local Memory Develop Different Representations Shared keys serve every later recursion, whereas local keys serve only the recursion that writes them. To see whether these roles are reflected in their representations, we compare S-size lt and lpt with three recursions, both trained with final loss, the only tested setting with at least three recursions where lt trains with final loss without a substantial drop in quality ( Figure 4 ). We evaluate both models on the same 4,096 4{,}096 -token validation sequence and extract queries and keys before rotary encoding. We concatenate the attention heads and fit principal component analysis (PCA) jointly to queries and keys across tokens and recursions per model and layer ( Appendix D ). Shared and local keys consistently form distinct clusters in lpt , whereas keys from different recursions overlap more in lt ( Figure 6 ). In Appendix D , we show similar separation in lpt across S and M at three and five recursions ( Figure 10 ). We also show that with full prediction caches, the clusters overlap more but still remain distinguishable, even though shared and local keys cover the same positions ( Figure 9 ). Prior work attributes the small cost of cache reuse to the similarity of keys and values across recursions ( Bae et al., 2025 ) , as we see in lt . With Memory Sharing, shared and local keys are instead clearly different. This shows that representation similarity across layers is not a necessary condition for effective memory sharing. This also fits the freedom that final loss gives: recursions need not all produce prediction-ready states, so the first can specialize in building memory and the later ones in using it. This specialization may help explain the quality gains, similar to how Monea et al. (2026) show that Transformers benefit from assigning memory construction and next-token prediction to separate residual streams. Takeaway 5. Shared and local memory diverge in their local representations, so sharing is not reliant on recursions writing similar memories. It predicts the next token, and it writes the keys and values that later positions read. Several architectures separate these jobs across token streams, as in the two-stream attention of XLNet ( Yang et al., 2019 ) . The State-Prediction Separation Transformer ( Monea et al., 2026 ) gives memory construction and next-token prediction separate residual streams and improves language modeling, and Langford et al. (2026) study a variant of this split. A second family separates them across layers. The first layers write one cache once, and the remaining layers only read it ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; Capps, 2026 ) . Instead, lpt decouples memory from prediction across the recursions of a looped Transformer: the first recursion writes the model’s only full-context memory, and every later recursion reads it while it predicts, keeping just a short window of its own. Looped models thus offer a third place for the split, with no extra stream or layer, and our analysis finds evidence that the recursions learn these roles ( Section 6 ). Looped Transformers and Memory Sharing Looped Transformers apply the same layers several times ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and recent work differs in which layers repeat and how recursions connect ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Mozer et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . In standard formulations, each recursion writes its own KV cache, so context memory grows with depth ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Sharing a cache across recursions, like sharing it across layers ( Brandon et al., 2024 ) , has been studied as a way to save memory. Without retraining, Huginn ( Geiping et al., 2025 ) reuses caches cyclically with little quality loss, and Ouro ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) can keep only the final or an averaged cache. Keeping only the first recursion’s cache sharply reduces Ouro’s quality, which suggests that shared memory has to be trained. Trained variants reuse the first recursion’s keys and values at a slight cost in quality ( Bae et al., 2025 ) , compute them once in a separate prelude ( Capps, 2026 ) , or learn gated or compressed caches ( Vendrell et al., 2026 ; O’Neill and Reid, 2026 ) . plt ( Wu et al., 2025 ) has the closest design to ours, although it focuses on parallelizing recursions. It shares the first recursion’s cache with gated local caches and runs recursions in parallel, while lpt keeps them sequential and reads both caches in one softmax. We find that lpt performs better. All of these treat sharing as a cost to contain. We instead treat it as an inductive bias that separates memory from prediction and show that it improves quality ( Section 5 and Section 6 ). 8 Discussion We investigate memory sharing as an architectural inductive bias for looped models, and find that it not only cuts context memory but also improves quality in both full attention and hybrid models. Our Memory Sharing lpt models achieve consistently better perplexity and downstream accuracy than their usual looped counterparts, while matching the KV cache memory of a standard non-looped model. Our analyses suggest that sharing helps recursions learn different roles. The first recursion builds memory that later recursions use to refine the prediction. Those reads also give the final loss a direct gradient path to the first recursion. The different representations of shared and local memory support this division of roles, and cutting this gradient path hurts learning. Shared memory changes how later recursions read information and how the first recursion learns to write it. Overall, our findings suggest that shared memory is a useful inductive bias for looped models, helping them make better use of computation within a limited memory budget. Limitations & Future work Like other looped Transformers, lpt is not compute-optimal: it trades time for quality, but unlike lt , its memory barely grows with depth. At five recursions it costs 4.3 4.3 – 4.8 × 4.8\times the decoding FLOPs of std , about the same as lt , and it spends the same number of recursions on every token. Choosing that number per token is future work. All our comparisons are parameter-matched, including deepstd , and we do not train a standard Transformer matched in decoding FLOPs instead, which at five recursions would have several times the parameters. We train up to 1 1 B parameters on one corpus with 4,096 4{,}096 -token contexts and do not test long-context tasks or, given our limited pretraining, very advanced tasks. Our analyses use S and M models, since not every configuration they need was trained at L, and only the detach ablation looks at training dynamics. Both the stability and memory improvements of lpt are promising for effectively scaling looped models to higher recursion counts. More sophisticated Memory Sharing approaches could also be explored in future work, such as increasing the number of state recursions or alternating state recursions and prediction recursions.
